claims.text: The nanoparticles are equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu particles with an initially homogeneous solid solution.
Premelting and melting in these nanoparticles are governed by temperature-induced heterogeneous surface segregation.
Cu and Ni migrate preferentially toward the nanoparticle surface during heating.
Cu and Ni are the lower-melting constituents relevant to formation of the segregated surface layer.
Heating produces a chemically inhomogeneous surface layer enriched primarily in Cu and Ni.
Surface segregation is accompanied by localized changes in atomic short-range order.
The segregated surface layer has a lower melting temperature than the nanoparticle core.
An enthalpic drive for elemental segregation locally overcomes the mixing-entropy contribution favoring a homogeneous solid solution during heating.
Composition enrichment and modified short-range order cause the surface region to premelt or soften before the core.
The core subsequently melts at a higher temperature, producing a two-step melting process.
Compared with single-metal or simpler-alloy nanoparticles, these HEA nanoparticles will show an earlier surface-softening, atomic-reordering, and segregation event followed by complete core melting.
The proposed single-metal or binary-alloy baseline exhibits a single sharp melting point.
The proposed baseline particles lack significant surface-segregation phenomena and therefore do not exhibit dual-stage melting.
Cooling will not fully restore the homogeneous solid solution, leaving detectable residual short-range chemical order.
The hypothesized behavior applies to equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles between 5 and 100 nm under controlled high-vacuum heating and cooling.
The behavior may change outside the specified composition and size range or under non-equilibrium thermal conditions.
Particle size and heating rate may alter the observed behavior.
